claims.text: Coupling ab initio thermodynamic integration with machine learning can accurately determine melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
The integrated approach can determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and associated liquid-phase properties.
Machine-learning acceleration makes the proposed approach computationally efficient.
The approach is applicable over a broad high-entropy-alloy compositional space.
High-entropy alloys in the initial state have multi-element disordered crystalline structures.
Ab initio thermodynamic integration can provide free-energy differences associated with melting.
Machine learning can interpolate and predict thermodynamic properties across different alloy compositions.
The proposed calculations and measurements are to be conducted near ambient pressure while traversing the melting-temperature regime.
Local chemical disorder and atomic-scale interactions influence high-entropy-alloy melting behavior.
First-principles calculations can accurately describe interatomic interactions and free-energy landscapes near melting.
Machine-learning interpolation accelerates exploration of alloy compositional space relative to calculating every composition directly.
Combining first-principles calculations and machine learning captures both local atomic interactions and global thermodynamic trends.
Predicted melting and liquid-state properties will agree with high-precision experiments within approximately 5–10%.
Existing computational approaches are computationally intensive and limited in compositional applicability.
Extreme local ordering or chemical clustering that is underrepresented in training data may reduce predictive performance.
The approach may be less predictive at non-ambient pressures or outside its calibrated temperature range.
No eligible cited record directly supports the feasibility or accuracy of the proposed combined approach.
The approach is falsified if prediction errors exceed 10% for a majority of the tested alloy compositions.
